summary: Kickoff to align on MSA execution path, procurement queue timing, and technical controls for private deployment. Key open items: DPA exceptions, KMS model, SLA uptime targets, and pricing anchoring for reserved capacity.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-03 14:00 UTC, 48 minutes. Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Oakbridge Procurement), Lisa Chen (Oakbridge Legal), Tom Alvarez (CTO), Renee Park (Eng Manager).

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate the time. Quick roll call, then we'll walk the playbook for MSA execution and how we slot into your procurement queue.
[00:20] Mark: Yeah hi, Mark here. We're hoping to get a clear path to sign off, we've got quarter-end constraints so timing matters.
[00:28] Lisa: Lisa here from legal. We'll want to focus on DPA redlines and the indemnity section.
[00:33] Tom: Tom, CTO — I'll speak to architecture and any on-prem constraints.
[00:38] Jordan: Great, Priya and I will run the execution steps. Priya, wanna start with the technical prerequisites?
[00:44] Priya: Sure. So from Redwood's side there are three deployment options: hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private deployment in your VPC. For Oakbridge given the data sensitivity you mentioned, we usually recommend Private (VPC) or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS.
[01:05] Renee: Quick clarification — when you say private, does that mean the control plane is in your tenancy or ours?
[01:12] Priya: Good question. For Private we provide a customer-controlled plane where the inference runtime sits in your VPC; control plane signals go over an encrypted channel but the data path stays private. There are two patterns: Redwood-hosted control-plane with VPC peering or fully customer-hosted control plane in an air-gapped setup for regulated use.
[01:35] Lisa: And KMS — can we bring our own key (HSM)? We need to log key usage for audits.
[01:41] Priya: Yes, BYOK is supported. We integrate with common cloud KMSs and also HSMs via KMIP in some cases. We'll capture key access logs; we'll also produce audit hooks that you can ingest into Splunk or your audit system.
[02:00] Jordan: From the MSA angle, the common asks we've seen are: DPA exceptions around subprocessor lists, SLA uptime percentages by environment, and data residency clauses. Lisa, are there specific triggers you need?
[02:15] Lisa: Indemnity limits and liability caps, plus a clearer definition of what constitutes 'customer data' — we've seen fuzzy language that could lead to a broadened claim. Also need to understand retention windows and data deletion procedures post-contract.
[02:35] Jordan: Understood. We can provide a redline-aware MSA template that flags those clauses. Historically Redwood offers standard liability caps tied to contract value and carve-outs for gross negligence.
[02:48] Mark: Our procurement board will also look at pricing anchoring: if we go to dedicated reserved capacity, what's the commit window and refund/exit mechanics?
[02:58] Priya: Typical reserved capacity commitments are 12 months or 36 months with graduated discounts. For exit mechanics, there's a ramp-down clause with notice; we can show a model that maps committed throughput to effective unit price. We'll include a sample pricing sheet.
[03:18] Tom: Performance question — with your private deployment, can we run internal benchmarks? We need a baseline latency P50/P95 at our expected concurrency.
[03:27] Priya: Absolutely. We do a bench run as part of the pilot: you provide a small sample workload and we run profiler traces. Note that results vary by model and sequence length; we'll include the KV cache warm-up assumptions.
[03:42] Renee: Also curious about network egress fees — if runtime is in our VPC but control plane sits with Redwood, are there any hidden egress costs?
[03:50] Jordan: We try to be explicit: when data stays in your region and VPC, egress is usually zero unless we move logs out. We'll note that in the pricing worksheet.
[04:03] Lisa: Back to DPA, will you accept a Customer-First subprocessor clause or do you require a fixed list?
[04:10] Jordan: We provide an Authorized Subprocessors list and a process to notify you prior to adding new ones. For enterprise customers we can negotiate a Customer-First approval flow for critical subprocessors.
[04:25] Mark: Timeline — what's realistic for us to get from redlines to signature? We have procurement committee meeting on 2026-10-20.
[04:32] Jordan: If we turn around the MSA template with inline comments within three business days and Lisa returns DPA exceptions within a week, we could target procurement finalization the week of 2026-10-18 — tight but feasible.
[04:48] Lisa: We'll try to prioritize. One more ask: do you provide SOC 2 Type II? Our audit team will require it.
[04:54] Priya: Yes, Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II. We'll share the latest attestation and a security packet; for private deployments we also provide architecture diagrams and KMS flow docs.
[05:07] Tom: Are there any SLA differentiators between Dedicated and Private? We care about failover and multi-AZ.
[05:13] Priya: Dedicated includes SLA-backed throughput and lower cost variance; Private lets you pin regions and control HA; SLA targets depend on the deployment topology — multi-AZ configs have higher uptime guarantees. We can propose an SLA matrix.
[05:30] Jordan: On procurement queueing — what things would block approval on your side? Mark?
[05:35] Mark: For us it's typically three things: legal signoff on MSA/DPA, clear pricing for the committed service, and an internal security sign-off. The security sign-off sometimes asks for a runbook showing incident response.
[05:50] Priya: We can share our incident response playbook summary and a runbook for escalation contacts.
[05:57] Lisa: I'm concerned about a broad audit rights clause. Can we limit audit to SOC reports and scheduled attestations rather than ad hoc deep-dives?
[06:07] Jordan: We can propose language that limits ad hoc audits and leans on attestations unless there's a substantiated incident. We'll annotate that option in the redline.
[06:18] Tom: One technical nit — how do you handle KV cache encryption at rest? Is the shard stored encrypted with customer key?
[06:27] Priya: KV stores are encrypted at rest; in private setups we can have keys under your KMS. In fully-hosted we use Redwood-managed keys but can move to BYOK on request. Some legacy models store cache differently and we'll document that.
[06:44] Renee: For the pilot, what's the minimum scope? We want to validate: latency, throughput, and privacy controls.
[06:50] Priya: Minimum viable pilot is 2 weeks: a small reserved pool, sample traffic, and a bench. We'll provide logs, latency metrics P50/P95/P99, and a short report.
[07:05] Mark: Pricing in the pilot — any costs?
[07:09] Jordan: We usually waive pilot fees for strategic deals but may ask for a nominal reservation if you want dedicated GPUs during the window. We'll propose a no-cost pilot first.
[07:19] Lisa: About data deletion: After termination, how do you ensure customer data removal in backups?
[07:26] Priya: We have data lifecycle policies; primary store deletion triggers a 30-day backup purge window unless you require immediate wipe which we can engineer with an extended runbook. We'll note options in the DPA section.
[07:44] Jordan: OK let's move into the procurement queue — Mark, how does your committee prefer artifacts? A single packet with MSA+pricing+security attestation?
[07:53] Mark: Single packet is preferred. It speeds review. We want a concise cover memo listing outstanding commercial items and legal waivers.
[08:01] Jordan: We'll prepare that. For pricing, what level of detail is needed to avoid gateway escalations?
[08:07] Mark: Show committed units, unit economics, and outage credits for SLA misses. Also show a clear path if we scale beyond committed capacity — how billing adjusts.
[08:18] Priya: We'll produce a pricing workbook that shows commit tiers and a sample invoice example with outage credits calculation.
[08:29] Lisa: Are there any export controls or data residency issues if Redwood routes models through different regions?
[08:36] Priya: We support region pinning; model serving will remain in pinned region if configured. Export control concerns are usually handled at the model and data classification level — we'll include a short note on model provenance.
[08:50] Tom: On the subject of subprocessors again, can you map which infra providers store logs vs those that run inference?
[08:57] Jordan: Yes, we'll provide an expanded subprocessor map showing function by vendor.
[09:02] Renee: One more question about SLAs — if we need a financial credit for downtime, what's the typical credit formula?
[09:09] Priya: Usually a percentage of monthly fees prorated against downtime buckets; e.g., P99-based uptime gets small credits, P95 larger. We'll include a sample schedule.
[09:23] Jordan: Great. I want to call out a few friction items we've seen that can slow procurement: unusual indemnity asks, unlimited audit windows, and BYOK proof-of-concept timing. If we can tab those early, we keep the pipeline moving.
[09:38] Lisa: Noted. We'll aim to be specific in our exceptions list.
[09:42] Mark: Can you confirm the specific docs you'll share after this call?
[09:46] Jordan: Yes: 1) Redline-ready MSA with inline commentary; 2) DPA draft and subprocessor map; 3) SOC 2 attestation and security packet; 4) Pricing workbook with reserved capacity examples; 5) Pilot runbook and technical diagram for VPC/KMS. Priya will handle 3 & 5.
[10:05] Priya: I'll also add a short note about KV cache handling and expected profiling artifacts.
[10:12] Lisa: About the MSA, do you accept a limitation on data processing to 'Performance of the Service' rather than 'any business purpose'?
[10:19] Jordan: We generally prefer 'performance of service' but can negotiate scopes around analytics and model improvement. For enterprise, we often carve model telemetry out unless the customer opts in.
[10:35] Tom: On telemetry, if we opt-out, does that impact performance tuning or cost?
[10:41] Priya: It reduces our ability to optimize across customers, but for a dedicated/private deployment we can run internal tuning without sending PII. Cost impact is minimal but we'll note operational tradeoffs.
[10:58] Renee: For the procurement packet, what level of contact info is included for incident response?
[11:03] Jordan: We'll include a named escalation ladder: primary SE contact (Priya), on-call ops, and AE contacts with RTO expectations.
[11:12] Mark: Ok, timeline check. If we receive the MSA on Tuesday and return redlines in a week, procurement meeting 10/20 looks possible.
[11:21] Jordan: Great. Anything else?
[11:24] Lisa: One small thing: SSL/TLS cipher suites — our security team sometimes flags older ciphers. Can you guarantee modern TLS 1.2+ and modern ciphers?
[11:34] Priya: Yes, we enforce TLS 1.2+ and prefer TLS 1.3; we'll include cipher suite details in the security packet.
[11:42] Tom: Regarding private deployment scale — if we need burst capacity for heavy inference days, how do you handle autoscale?
[11:50] Priya: There's a burst capacity model where we allow short-term scale up to a certain multiplier; that has a price premium but it's available. We'll document parameters.
[12:03] Jordan: OK we'll wrap. Recap: Redwood sends MSA with inline notes (Jordan), Priya sends security and VPC diagrams, Oakbridge to return DPA exceptions, procurement to target 10/20 meeting.
[12:16] Mark: Sounds good. We'll push legal to prioritize.
[12:20] Lisa: I'll aim to send the exceptions by 10/13.
[12:24] Jordan: Thanks all. Priya and I will get the packet over by Tuesday EOD.
[12:30] Tom: Thanks, bye.

End of meeting — Action items and next steps captured.
